verdicts.why: The negative lookahead (?!\S*\.beacon\.internal) is unbounded: \S* spans the entire URL token, so any occurrence of .beacon.internal anywhere in the non-space run kills the match. I ran the regex: 'https://evil.example/aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa' matches, 'https://evil.example/aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa?x=.beacon.internal' does not. So the rule can be walked past by appending the internal marker as a query fragment or path segment. Shadow mode today (beacon.yaml:32) is why it blocks nothing now, but the assertion is explicitly about the rule being useless once mode flips to enforce, and _screen (assistant.py:45) does raise in that mode.

verdicts.why: The trust policy names Principal AWS '*' - any AWS principal in any account may call sts:AssumeRole - with only sts:ExternalId and aws:SecureTransport as conditions. The external id is a shared secret, not an identity, so anyone who obtains it (partners routinely paste them into tickets and pipelines) assumes the role from an account of their choosing. The role is not toothless: the reports bucket policy grants it GetObject and ListBucket over the whole bucket.

searched.found: none - Principal is the literal '*'

searched.for: what the role can actually reach

verdicts.why: All four ECS task roles are created with the same trust policy: Principal Service ecs-tasks.amazonaws.com, sts:AssumeRole, and no Condition block at all - no aws:SourceAccount, no aws:SourceArn, which is the condition AWS documents for this exact resource. Nothing else in the stack supplies it: there is no permission boundary, no SCP, and the extra RolePolicy in index.ts only scopes what the role can do, not who may assume it. The impact is confused-deputy hardening rather than a direct path, but the control is simply absent and nothing substitutes for it.

verdicts.why: mintServiceToken signs with process.env.SERVICE_TOKEN_KEY ?? 'local-development-key', on a live route (POST /oauth/token wired at index.ts:27, and given its own location in the edge config). Nothing anywhere in the tree sets SERVICE_TOKEN_KEY, and the guard immediately above - refusing a client whose secret is empty - shows the author closing exactly this class of insecure default one line earlier, so the fallback here is unguarded by design. I did find that this API's own bearer path verifies against a remote JWKS, which cannot accept an HS256 token; that breaks the verify half of the feature rather than protecting the key, and the tokens minted with a key published in source are still handed to the billing-sync and usage-rollup clients over the wire.

searched.for: a deployment manifest, env file or default that supplies the real key
searched.found: the single reference at auth.ts:99 - nothing sets it

searched.for: the verifier for these tokens
searched.found: actorFromBearer verifies against createRemoteJWKSet, which rejects symmetric algorithms - so a forged HS256 token does not authenticate to this API; the consumer that does accept them is outside the tree

searched.for: a guard that refuses to mint when the key is missing

verdicts.why: The incremental predicate is created_at > max(created_at), so any source row sharing the exact maximum timestamp with the previous run is never read again - it falls outside both the old run (not yet inserted) and the next one (not strictly greater). The masked customer model repeats the same pattern on updated_at.

searched.for: a lookback/overlap macro applied to incremental models
searched.found: the only staging hooks are enable_row_security and apply_grants

verdicts.why: In staging both branches fire, and both construct an aws.s3.BucketPolicy against the same bucket id. S3 keeps exactly one policy per bucket, so the two resources overwrite each other and the effective policy is whichever PutBucketPolicy landed last - a non-deterministic security outcome that also drifts on every refresh. Nothing sequences or merges them: there is no dependsOn, and the two policies have different Pulumi names, so the engine treats them as independent.

verdicts.why: The template can never arrive. printQuery is declared .strict(), and Hono's query validator hands zod every query parameter present on the request, not just the declared ones - so a request carrying ?template=... fails the schema and @hono/zod-validator returns 400 before the handler body runs. c.req.query('template') is therefore always undefined and new Function only ever compiles DEFAULT_SHEET, a fixed literal. There is no other route, header or body path into that expression.

searched.for: whether the query schema admits an unknown key
searched.found: .strict() on printQuery - an unrecognised key is a validation error, and zValidator answers 400 on failure before invoking the handler

searched.for: another way to reach the compiler with attacker text
searched.found: only this route; DEFAULT_SHEET is the sole fallback value

searched.for: a middleware that might rewrite or strip the query before validation
searched.found: requireAuth and the legacy attachments mount only - nothing that would let template bypass the validator
